title: Writing a value-led message and checking your claims
audience: Trainers, instructors and therapists who write promotional material, web pages or social posts
learningOutcomes: Rewrite a list of features as client-facing benefits
State a unique selling point in one sentence and apply it to a headline and one closing prompt
Identify claims that need evidence, written permission or a legal check before publication

instruction.heading: Lead with the outcome, then the method
instruction.body: Clients buy a result they can picture, along with how the process feels. A feature names what you do, such as a 45-minute circuit. A benefit names what changes for the person, such as climbing stairs without planning rest stops. Turn each feature into a benefit by asking what the client would notice in their week. Put the benefit first in every headline, post and flyer, and keep the method as supporting detail.

instruction.heading: One unique selling point, stated once
instruction.body: The unique selling point is the single reason a prospect would choose you over another option. It must be true, specific and provable in your own practice. Write it as one sentence and use the same sentence across channels. If you cannot state it in one sentence, the offer is not clear enough yet.

instruction.heading: Claims need evidence, consent and a legal check
instruction.body: Advertising must not mislead. Claims about results, such as weight loss, pain relief or body shape, need evidence you can show and must not promise outcomes that depend on the person. Testimonials and before-and-after images need the person's written permission and must reflect a real experience. The Australian Consumer Law turns on whether conduct is misleading or deceptive.

instruction.heading: Headline and closing prompt
instruction.body: A headline says who you help and the outcome, in one line. The sub-heading names the service area and the format. The closing prompt is one clear next step, such as booking a first session. Avoid competing actions on one page, and keep any testimonial block to genuine, permitted quotes.

procedure: List every feature of your main service.
Turn each feature into a benefit a client would notice within a month.
Write the unique selling point sentence and check that it is true and specific.
Draft a headline, a sub-heading and one closing prompt.
Review each claim for evidence, written permission and scope. Hold back any unresolved claim until it is checked.

workedExamples.situation: A hypothetical mobile massage therapist drafts a flyer that says the treatment is guaranteed to fix back pain in three sessions.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the therapist change before printing?
workedExamples.reasoning: The guarantee and the outcome promise cannot be backed by evidence for every client, and the wording implies a treatment result. Replace it with what the session includes, state that results vary, and remove the guarantee. Check the final wording against ACCC guidance.

equipmentAndPpe: Claims checklist with one row per claim and its evidence location
Signed permission form for testimonials and images

commonErrors.error: Promising guaranteed results or a fixed outcome
commonErrors.prevention: Describe what the session includes and say results vary between people.

commonErrors.error: Publishing a testimonial without permission, or with an invented name
commonErrors.prevention: Keep a dated, signed permission for every testimonial and use only genuine quotes.

commonErrors.error: Using before-and-after images without consent, or edited so the result looks different
commonErrors.prevention: Use only images the client has agreed to, and store the consent.

commonErrors.error: Several competing calls to action on one page
commonErrors.prevention: Keep one closing prompt per page.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Australian Consumer Law: misleading or deceptive conduct and false representations in advertising. Check ACCC guidance before publishing fitness and massage wording.
Wording that implies diagnosing, treating or curing a medical condition may sit outside a fitness or massage service.
This lesson does not grant authority to make health claims and does not grant any licence or registration.

qualityStandard: Every headline and offer states an outcome the service can plausibly deliver and that has evidence on file
Every testimonial and image has dated written permission on file
Each unchecked claim is held back until checked
documentationEvidence: Claims checklist with an evidence reference per claim
summary: Lead with the benefit; keep the method in support.
One unique selling point, one closing prompt.
Check every claim for evidence, permission and legal risk before it goes out.

knowledgeChecks.question: A unique selling point is best described as:
options: A list of all your features and what each one costs the client
The one true reason a prospect should choose you, in one sentence
A discount offer that is repeated across every product line

knowledgeChecks.question: When may a testimonial be used in marketing?
options: When a friend writes it so it sounds real and nobody checks it
When it is genuine and the client has given written permission
When it shows a result you cannot evidence for the client

knowledgeChecks.question: Which headline follows the approach in this lesson?
options: Premium trainer for everyone who wants the best results for less money
Strength sessions for busy parents in one named suburb, with a fixed start time
Guaranteed weight loss in one week with no diet or effort needed at all

officialReferences.title: Advertising and selling guide: A guide for business (ACCC)
officialReferences.covers: Advertising and selling guide (ACCC, July 2021), read in full in this pass. Misleading conduct is judged by the overall impression created, and conduct can mislead by silence or omission; fine print is taken into account. Claims must be substantiated, and the guide says a business must have reasonable grounds for making them at the time. For health and medical products it expects accurate and truthful information. The guide does not mention fitness, gym or personal training claims; its only gym example is in the unfair contract terms section. How these rules apply to fitness or massage wording: UNCONFIRMED; check current ACCC guidance before publication. Publisher: ACCC.
